what does it mean when you say "pull the ground up" (or down)?

what does it mean when you say "pull the ground up" (or down)?

Ground, or the cathode, is assumed to have the potential of zero. This is important for amplifiers, as their core feature is to compare a 'positive' and a 'negative', and compensate for the difference. One way to use this feature is in a negative feed back loop, which is the most basic for signal amplification. In it, the 'positive' is grounded. If the ground gets noisy, the amplifier will respond to the noise (a natural response, depending on the frequency of the noise, they will settle on the mean frequency, otherwise known as the tone you are hearing) amplify the 'negative' (your audio signal). Because now there is a difference between the 'positive' or 'negative' the amplifier will either sink (deliver negative potential difference) or gain its output (positive potential difference) to compensate.

For simplicity, an ideal situation when your audio system is not receiving any signal is that the 'positive' and 'negative' match. When you send a signal down the negative, the amplifier will respond to the difference to the positive and negative, the amplifier will gain on that signal. By turning the volume knob up, you are increasing the resistance in the feedback part, reducing the feedback. The amplifier will compensate by delivering a louder signal.

Anyway, now we have noise due to induction in the system. Therefore the 'positive', has risen as well. Because of this noise, affecting the comparison the amplifier needs, it technically gets inversely convoluted with the signal you want.

This is why having separate grounds is important for signal work, and your audio, instead of multiple lines all running to one ground.
